extracted.intended_audience: crisis managers, public relations practitioners, organizational communicators, and scholars of crisis communication
extracted.subtask_description: Applying Situational Crisis Communication Theory (SCCT) to assess a crisis situation and choose post-crisis communication strategies that protect organizational reputation while addressing stakeholder needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical priority: protect stakeholders first
rubrics_metrics.description: The first priority in any crisis is to protect stakeholders from harm, not to protect the reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin crisis communication by addressing physical threats with instructing information (what stakeholders must do to protect themselves) and psychological threats with adapting information (information to cope and corrective actions). Expressions of concern for victims are recommended and expected but are not admissions of guilt. Only after meeting these obligations should managers focus on reputational assets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use evidence-based crisis communication guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence-based guidance for decision making in a crisis must be supported by scientific evidence from empirical research rather than personal preference and unscientific experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SCCT relies on experimental methods instead of case studies; use empirical findings (e.g., tested relationships between crisis types, attributions, emotions, and reputational outcomes) to guide strategy selection rather than intuition or solely anecdotal case analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial crisis responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial crisis responsibility is a function of stakeholder attributions of personal control for the crisis by the organization — how much stakeholders believe organizational actions caused the crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how stakeholders are likely to attribute responsibility based on the crisis type/frame. Greater perceived organizational responsibility increases reputational threat and negative emotions; strategy selection should reflect this assessed level of responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis history (intensifying factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis history is whether or not an organization has had a similar crisis in the past; a past similar crisis suggests an ongoing problem and intensifies attributions of responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the organization has a history of similar crises, anticipate stronger attributions of responsibility and greater reputational damage; this can escalate the recommended level of accommodation in response strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior relational reputation (intensifying factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior relational reputation is how well or poorly an organization is perceived to have treated stakeholders in other contexts; an unfavorable prior relational reputation intensifies crisis responsibility attributions and reputational threat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider stakeholders' prior views: an unfavorable relationship history increases direct and indirect reputational damage and may require more accommodative or reparative strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis types / clusters (victim, accidental, intentional)
rubrics_metrics.description: SCCT identifies three crisis clusters based on attributions of crisis responsibility: (1) victim cluster — very weak attributions of responsibility (natural disasters, product tampering, rumor); (2) accidental cluster — minimal attributions (technical-error accident, unintentional harm); (3) intentional cluster — very strong attributions (human-error product harm, organizational misdeed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the crisis type/frame because it predicts the initial level of crisis responsibility stakeholders will attribute to the organization; use examples and cues (external agent, accidental vs. intentional, technical vs human error) to classify the crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step process for evaluating reputational threat
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis managers first determine the initial crisis responsibility via crisis type, then apply intensifying factors (crisis history and prior relational reputation) to adjust the reputational threat assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 1: identify crisis type to set initial responsibility level. Step 2: factor in crisis history and prior relational reputation to escalate or moderate the threat. Use this assessed threat level to guide the selection of crisis response strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for emotional reactions (anger and sympathy) and behavioral intentions
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribution processes evoke emotions — anger and sympathy — which drive behavioral responses; increased attributions of responsibility generate stronger anger (and sometimes schadenfreude) and reduce sympathy, which can lead to negative word of mouth or severed relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the affective consequences of perceived responsibility: strategies should aim to reduce negative affect (anger) and support positive behavioral intentions (purchase, support). Measure or anticipate stakeholders' emotions as part of strategy selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three objectives of crisis response strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis response strategies have three objectives relative to protecting reputations: (1) shape attributions of the crisis, (2) change perceptions of the organization in crisis, and (3) reduce the negative affect generated by the crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing responses, evaluate how well each tactic will (a) influence causal attributions, (b) present or restore organizational character, and (c) reduce stakeholders' anger or other negative emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial strategies (primary group)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deny strategies attempt to remove any connection between the organization and the crisis — establishing a 'no crisis' frame or refuting charges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most useful in rumor and challenge crises where establishing that there is no real crisis can spare reputational harm. Risk: denial only works if stakeholders and media accept the no-crisis frame. Use when evidence supports denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diminish strategies (primary group)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diminish strategies argue that the crisis is not as bad as perceived or that the organization lacked control over the crisis, thereby lessening the organization's connection to the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to reframe the event as accidental or outside organizational control; reinforce existing frames rather than attempt wholly new frames. Require solid evidence; ineffective if media or online voices reject the frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuild strategies (primary group)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebuild strategies attempt to improve the organization's reputation by offering material and/or symbolic aid to victims (e.g., compensation, full apology) and taking positive actions to offset the crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate for crises presenting severe reputational threat (intentional cluster or accidental events with intensifying factors). Rebuild generates new reputational assets but is costlier; match rebuild level to threat to avoid unnecessary expense or backfire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjusting information (instructing and adapting information)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjusting information consists of instructing information (to protect stakeholders from physical harm) and adapting information (to help stakeholders cope psychologically and learn corrective actions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver instructions directly or via media (e.g., recalls, sirens) and provide corrective action details and expressions of concern to reduce psychological stress. Adjusting information is ethically required and also helps reduce negative affect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bolstering strategies (supplemental)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bolstering offers minimal opportunity to develop reputational assets via praising stakeholders, reminding of past good works, or invoking victimage to draw sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best used as supplements to primary strategies and adjusting information. Reminder requires credible past good works; victimage can evoke sympathy if the organization legitimately is a victim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match accomodativeness of response to reputational threat
rubrics_metrics.description: SCCT recommends that as the reputational threat and negative affect increase, crisis managers should utilize crisis response strategies with the requisite level of accepting crisis responsibility; do not over-accommodate unnecessarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using overly accommodative strategies when not indicated—these are more expensive and may produce no greater reputational benefit or may worsen perceptions (stakeholders may infer the crisis is worse if response is excessively strong). If financial or other constraints prevent the recommended strategy, use the next-best option and be aware of diminished reparative effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider boundary conditions (financial constraints, media frame, online dynamics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines are affected by constraints surrounding the crisis situation: financial resources, how the news media or online actors frame the crisis, and whether managers can change that frame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unable to afford the recommended response, select the most effective affordable alternative. Recognize that media frames and online postings often determine stakeholder frames — managers may be forced to operate within an externally set frame, or have an easier time if no clear frame exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use communication to establish or influence crisis frames
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis managers use response strategies to establish a frame or reinforce an existing frame; the media (or online posters) are often the final arbiters of the adopted frame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present 'your side of the story' to news media; for online-dominant crises, monitor and engage with internet posters, influential bloggers, critics, and victims to influence the circulating frames. Framing cues—external cause, intent, technical vs human error—shape attributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be strategic about reducing negative affect (anger) through adjusting and rebuild actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjusting information (expressing concern) and rebuild strategies (compensation, apology) are the most effective ways to reduce negative affect and blunt stakeholder anger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize expressions of concern and corrective actions to reduce psychological stress; pair with appropriate material remedies (compensation) or apologies depending on assessed responsibility and intensifying factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on case-study speculation; prefer testable conceptual links
rubrics_metrics.description: SCCT demands a theoretical link between crisis situations and crisis response strategies and critiques image restoration case studies as speculative and lacking conceptual linkage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer strategies justified by tested theoretical connections (how situation variables predict attributions and how responses affect those attributions) rather than selecting tactics solely because they appeared to work in a case study.
